What can be soldOn 27 October 2026

  1. AI chips up to the H200

    US → China

    Case by case

    Case by case below 21,000 TPP and 6,500 GB/s of memory bandwidth, with conditions

    from 15 Jan 2026 · announced 13 Jan 2026 · 91 FR 1684 · 15 CFR 742.6(b)(10)(iii) · Entry in the timeline

    Data center accelerators up to the H200's level: the A100 and H100, the cut-down A800, H800 and H20, the H200 and AMD's MI325X. Since 15 January 2026, license applications to export chips below 21,000 TPP and 6,500 GB/s of memory bandwidth from the United States to China or Macau are reviewed case by case. The exporter must certify, among other things, that US supply is sufficient and that a third party in the United States has tested the chips.

  2. AI chips above the H200 band

    US → China

    Presumption of denial

    Denial stays for chips at or above 21,000 TPP or 6,500 GB/s of memory bandwidth

    from 15 Jan 2026 · announced 13 Jan 2026 · 91 FR 1684 · 15 CFR 742.6(b)(10)(iii) · Entry in the timeline

    Data center accelerators at 21,000 TPP or more, or with 6,500 GB/s or more of memory bandwidth, such as Nvidia's Blackwell B200. License applications to export them to China or Macau are reviewed with a presumption of denial.

  3. Chipmaking tools

    US → China

    Case by case

    Foreign-owned fabs in China lose their blanket approval for US tools (VEU)

    from 31 Dec 2025 · announced 29 Aug 2025 · 90 FR 42321 · 15 CFR part 748, supplement no. 7 · Entry in the timeline

    Semiconductor manufacturing equipment and the software that runs it. A license is needed. Applications for advanced fabs meet a presumption of denial, and the rest are reviewed case by case.

  4. Dutch and Japanese controls

    Netherlands and Japan → China

    Case by case

    Japan adds more chipmaking tools, such as etch, deposition and inspection tools, to its license list

    from 28 May 2025 · announced 28 Mar 2025 · Cabinet Order No. 102 of 2025 and METI Ordinance No. 34 of 2025 · Entry in the timeline

    Advanced immersion DUV scanners (machines that print chip patterns) and some measuring and inspection tools from the Netherlands, and the chipmaking equipment Japan added to its license list in 2023 and 2025. The Dutch controls cover exports to every destination outside the EU, and the Japanese controls cover every destination.

  5. High-bandwidth memory

    US → China, including HBM made abroad

    Presumption of denial

    Denial for Chinese-headquartered buyers, approval for the rest

    from 31 Dec 2024 · announced 2 Dec 2024 · 89 FR 96790 · 15 CFR 742.6(a)(6)(i)(B), (b)(10)(ii); 740.25 · Entry in the timeline

    Memory stacks with more than 2 GB per second of bandwidth per square millimeter, wherever they are made, including foreign stacks that the direct product rule brings under US control. The license requirement covers only Macau and Country Group D:5, the US list of arms-embargoed countries that includes China. For buyers in China or Macau, approval is presumed if they are headquartered elsewhere, and denial if they are headquartered there. License Exception HBM still lets an exporter in the US or in Country Group A:5, a group of close US partners, ship stacks below 3.3 GB per second per square millimeter without a license. The stacks must go directly to a packaging site for the designer that bought them.

  10. AI chips to the rest of the world

    US → every other destination

    Case by case

    UAE joins Country Group A:5, and shipments to named recipients need no license

    from 10 Jul 2026 · announced 14 Jul 2026 · 91 FR 43034 · 15 CFR 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A) and (B); supplement no. 8 to part 740 · Entry in the timeline

    The top band of accelerators, ECCNs 3A090.a and 4A090.a, which need a license to or within any destination worldwide under the AI Diffusion Rule of January 2025. BIS stopped enforcing the rule in May 2025 and said it would issue a replacement. In the rule, License Exception AIA lets exporters ship them without a license to nineteen destinations, the United States and eighteen allies, listed in supplement no. 5 to part 740. License Exception LPP allows up to 26,900,000 TPP a year per recipient elsewhere. License applications for the nineteen are reviewed with a presumption of approval. The rest count against a cap of 790,000,000 TPP per country through 2027.

  11. Money, stakes and tariffs

    at home

    Policy

    Taiwan wins tariff relief and pledges $250 billion of investment

    from 15 Jan 2026 · www.federalregister.gov · Entry in the timeline

    Subsidies, state investment funds, government stakes in companies, procurement bars and tariffs. None of these is a license requirement.

  • No licenseNone needed.
  • RestrictedA government limits sales to some buyers or uses without banning them outright.
  • Case by caseA license is required, and each application is judged on its own.
  • Presumption of denialA license is required and will normally be refused. This is the usual policy for those on the Entity List, a US list of restricted foreign companies, institutes and individuals.
  • ProhibitedNo license is available, or the item is banned outright.
  • PolicyMoney and tariffs, which do not stop a shipment.
  • SuspendedThe rule is on hold until the date shown. When the hold ends, the state beside it takes effect.

20183 moves

  1. 15 Apr 2018US (BIS)

    US export control · Denial order

    ZTE denial order activated

    The first time one US order halted most of a large Chinese electronics firm's production.

    The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the US Commerce Department's export control office, activated a suspended denial order against ZTE, a Chinese maker of telecom equipment and phones. The order was set to run for seven years, to March 2025. BIS had found that the company lied about disciplining the employees responsible for illegal shipments to Iran and North Korea. The order barred all US persons from exporting anything to ZTE. The ban cut off ZTE's supply of Qualcomm processors and its Android licensing, and most of its production stopped within weeks. ZTE settled on 8 June for a $1 billion penalty plus $400 million in escrow, a replaced board and a US-appointed compliance monitor.

    83 FR 17644 · 15 CFR part 766www.federalregister.gov

  2. 13 Jul 2018US (BIS)

    US export control · Denial order

    ZTE denial order terminated

    The only outright US export ban on this timeline ended in July 2018 after a settlement.

    BIS terminated the April 2018 denial order and removed ZTE from the Denied Persons List. ZTE had met the terms of its 8 June settlement: a $1 billion penalty, $400 million placed in escrow, a replaced board and a US-appointed compliance monitor. A ten-year denial order remains in place but suspended. The April order is the only US measure on this timeline that barred exports outright.

    83 FR 34825 · 15 CFR part 766www.govinfo.gov

  3. 30 Oct 2018US (BIS)

    US export control · Listing

    Fujian Jinhua added to the Entity List

    US toolmakers stopped deliveries mid-installation, and Jinhua's DRAM fab never reached volume production.

    BIS added Fujian Jinhua Integrated Circuit, a state-backed DRAM memory-chip start-up, to the Entity List, a US list of foreign parties that need a license to receive some or all US-regulated items. Jinhua's entry required a license, with a presumption of denial, for all items subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR), the US rules on commercial exports. The End-User Review Committee said the firm posed a significant risk of activities contrary to US national security. BIS separately warned that new Chinese DRAM capacity threatened the viability of US suppliers of military memory. The listing stopped deliveries of Applied Materials, Lam and KLA tools mid-installation, and the fab never reached volume production. It was the first use of the Entity List against a Chinese memory maker and the model for later chip listings.

    83 FR 54519 · 15 CFR 744.11www.federalregister.gov

20194 moves

  1. 16 May 2019US (BIS)

    US export control · Listing

    Huawei and 68 affiliates added to the Entity List

    US suppliers needed a license to sell Huawei anything, chips included.

    BIS listed Huawei Technologies and 68 non-US affiliates across 26 destinations, requiring a license with a presumption of denial for every item subject to the EAR. The listing ended Huawei's access to Google Mobile Services, Intel and Xilinx parts and US chip design (EDA) software. BIS added a further 46 affiliates in August 2019 and 38 more in August 2020.

    84 FR 22961 · 15 CFR 744.11www.federalregister.gov

  2. 1 Jul 2019in force 4 Jul 2019Japan (METI)

    Other governments · License policy

    Japan requires individual licenses for three chemicals sold to South Korea

    Each export of the three chemicals to South Korea needed its own license from 4 July 2019.

    From 4 July 2019, Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) required exporters to get an individual license to ship fluorinated polyimide, resist (photoresist) and hydrogen fluoride to South Korea. The bulk licenses that had covered the three items no longer applied. The change also covered their technology, which METI said may include technology transferred with exports of manufacturing equipment. METI said the relationship of trust with South Korea, including on export control, "has been significantly undermined". It also said it had found sensitive items exported to South Korea with inadequate management by companies. On the same day METI opened public comment on removing South Korea from its list of so-called white countries.

    Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act, articles 25(1) and 48(1)web.archive.org

  3. 2 Aug 2019in force 28 Aug 2019Japan (METI)

    Other governments · Rule

    Japan removes South Korea from its preferred trade partner list

    South Korea lost access to Japan's general bulk licenses, and exports to it came under catch-all control.

    The Japanese cabinet approved an order removing South Korea from Appended Table III of the Export Trade Control Order, the countries often called the white list or preferred trade partner list. The order was promulgated on 7 August and took effect on 28 August 2019. Exporters could no longer use general bulk licenses for goods and technology sent to South Korea. Those exports also came under catch-all control, which requires a license for unlisted goods and technology that could have military uses or serve weapons of mass destruction. Special general bulk licenses, granted to exporters that meet higher standards, remained available. METI regrouped destinations into Groups A to D and placed South Korea in Group B. Fluorinated polyimide, resist and hydrogen fluoride had needed individual licenses since 4 July. METI said it would grant them if exports were verified as legitimate private transactions.

    Export Trade Control Order (Cabinet Order No. 378 of 1949), Appended Table IIIweb.archive.org

  4. 18 Sep 2019South Korea (MOTIE)

    Other governments · Rule

    South Korea removes Japan from its white list

    South Korea dropped Japan from its own fast-track trade list and took Japan's export curbs to the WTO.

    South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy (MOTIE) removed Japan from its white list of countries with fast-track trade status, with immediate effect on 18 September 2019. South Korean exports to Japan related to weapons production faced longer permit applications and more paperwork. The ministry said the change aimed to improve South Korea's export control system and was not retaliation against Japan. Japan had removed South Korea's fast-track status in late August, after tightening exports to South Korea of three materials used in the chip and display industries. South Korea had also filed a World Trade Organization (WTO) dispute over the Japanese export curbs.

    www.reuters.com

20204 moves

  1. 15 May 2020US (BIS)

    US export control · Rule

    Foreign Direct Product Rule extended to Huawei chip designs

    Washington used control of US design tools to stop TSMC building Huawei's chips.

    BIS amended General Prohibition Three, the foreign direct product rule. Foreign-made chips designed by Huawei or its chip unit HiSilicon became subject to the EAR when they were the direct product of US-origin software or technology. The rule covered HiSilicon's Kirin phone chips and Ascend AI chips made by TSMC, the Taiwanese contract chipmaker, even though the chips contained no US content. TSMC stopped taking new HiSilicon orders within days and stopped shipments after 14 September 2020. This was the first time Washington used control of US design tools to stop a foreign foundry serving a foreign customer.

    85 FR 29849 · 15 CFR 736.2(b)(3)(vi)www.federalregister.gov

  2. 17 Aug 2020US (BIS)

    US export control · Rule

    Huawei FDPR broadened to any chip made with US equipment

    Because almost every advanced fab runs American tools, even off-the-shelf chips became unavailable to Huawei.

    BIS widened the May 2020 rule so that any foreign-produced item made with US-origin semiconductor equipment or software needs a license when Huawei is a party to the transaction. The requirement applies whatever firm designed the item. BIS also added 38 more Huawei affiliates in 21 countries and let the Temporary General License expire. Because almost every advanced fab uses Applied Materials, Lam or KLA tools, the rule made even off-the-shelf chips unavailable to Huawei. This rule created the equipment-based direct product test that BIS reused two years later in its China-wide rules.

    85 FR 51596 · 15 CFR 736.2(b)(3)(vi); 744.11www.federalregister.gov

  3. 17 Oct 2020in force 1 Dec 2020China (NPC Standing Committee)

    China · Rule

    China's Export Control Law

    The law behind every Chinese export control since 2020, from gallium licensing in 2023 to rare earth rules in 2025.

    The Standing Committee of the National People's Congress adopted a single statute for export control, in force from 1 December 2020. It authorizes control lists, licenses, and end-user and end-use certificates. It also authorizes a list of foreign parties that may be barred from buying, controls over reexports of Chinese-origin items, and countermeasures against states that use export controls against China. Every Chinese export control since, from the gallium licensing of 2023 to the rare earth rules of 2025, has been issued under it.

    Export Control Law of the People’s Republic of China, article 49exportcontrol.mofcom.gov.cn

  4. 18 Dec 2020US (BIS)

    US export control · Listing

    SMIC added to the Entity List

    The listing ended SMIC's plan to buy an EUV scanner, but SMIC still reached 7 nm with DUV immersion scanners.

    BIS added the Chinese chipmaker Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC) and ten related entities to the Entity List. It cited China's military-civil fusion doctrine and evidence of activities between SMIC and entities of concern in the Chinese military industrial complex. Licenses for items uniquely required for production at 10 nm and below carry a presumption of denial, while less advanced items are reviewed case by case. The listing ended SMIC's plan to buy an extreme ultraviolet (EUV) scanner, a machine that prints chip patterns, from the Dutch firm ASML. The Dutch government had been withholding a license for that scanner since 2019. Even so, by 2022 SMIC had reached a 7 nm-class node with deep ultraviolet (DUV) immersion scanners, printing its finest layers in several passes.

    85 FR 83416 · 15 CFR 744.11www.federalregister.gov

20212 moves

  1. 9 Sep 2021EU (Parliament and Council)

    Other governments · Rule

    EU's new dual-use export regulation enters into force

    The EU's dual-use export rules took effect, letting the Commission update the control list by delegated act.

    The European Union's new Export Control Regulation for dual-use items, civilian goods and technology with possible military or security uses, entered into force on 9 September 2021. It replaced the EU's 2009 rules. The European Commission said the regulation builds on the Wassenaar Arrangement, the multilateral export control framework behind many of the restrictions it imposes. The regulation lets the Commission amend the list of controlled items or destinations by delegated act, a simplified procedure. The Commission said the new framework would also let the EU pool expertise on emerging dual-use technologies such as advanced computing.

    Regulation (EU) 2021/821ec.europa.eu

  2. 23 Nov 2021Italy (government)

    Other governments · Screening

    Italy vetoes a Chinese purchase of Applied Materials' Italian unit

    Italy blocked a Chinese firm from buying an Applied Materials unit after the industry minister cited the semiconductor sector.

    Italy's government blocked Zhejiang Jingsheng Mechanical, a Chinese company, from buying Applied Materials' screen printing equipment business in Italy through a joint venture with the US group's Hong Kong arm. Zhejiang Jingsheng disclosed the veto in a Hong Kong filing on 23 November 2021. Two government sources told Reuters the cabinet had decided on 18 November on the recommendation of Industry Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti. The sources said Giorgetti had argued that the takeover could have consequences for the strategic semiconductor sector. The joint venture was also meant to take over Applied Materials' wafer equipment business in Singapore and its assets in China. In April 2021 the government had stopped Shenzhen Invenland Holdings, another Chinese company, from buying a controlling stake in a maker of semiconductor equipment. Italy uses its golden powers to block bids in industries it considers strategic.

    www.reuters.com

    Industrial policy · Policy

    CHIPS and Science Act signed

    Federal money for American fabs came with a ten-year bar on expanding capacity in China.

    Public Law 117-167 authorized $52.7 billion for US semiconductors, including $39 billion in manufacturing incentives, $13.2 billion for R&D and workforce and $500 million for international supply-chain work. The law also provided a 25 percent advanced manufacturing investment tax credit. Companies taking incentives are barred for ten years from materially expanding advanced capacity in China or other countries of concern. Commerce's final awards included about $6.6 billion for TSMC Arizona, $4.745 billion for Samsung's Texas sites and $7.86 billion for Intel.

    Public Law 117-167www.govinfo.gov

    US export control · Rule

    License requirement on design software for gate-all-around chips

    Software for designing the newest transistor structure needed a license from October 2022, years before BIS's 2025 letters on chip-design software.

    In December 2021 the Wassenaar Arrangement, the forum in which governments agree common export control lists, decided to control four emerging technologies. BIS wrote those decisions into US rules. For one of them it created ECCN 3D006, a new entry in the US list of controlled items. The entry put a national-security license requirement on electronic computer-aided design software specially designed for developing integrated circuits with gate-all-around transistors. The rule called that transistor structure key to processes at 3 nm and below. The rule was published on 15 August 2022, and the 3D006 control took effect on 14 October 2022. The requirement covers exports to China.

    87 FR 49979 · 15 CFR part 774, supplement no. 1 (ECCN 3D006)www.federalregister.gov

    US export control · License policy

    First license requirement on A100 and H100 exports to China

    Nvidia needed a license to sell its top chips in China and answered within weeks with the cut-down A800.

    Nvidia disclosed in an 8-K filing that the US government had imposed a new license requirement on 26 August 2022. It covered exports of the A100, the A100X and the forthcoming H100 to China, Hong Kong and Russia. It also covered DGX systems built on those chips and any future chip at equivalent performance. Nvidia said about $400 million of third-quarter China sales were at risk. AMD received a parallel restriction on the MI250. Within weeks Nvidia offered the A800, which kept the A100's computing power but cut its interconnect bandwidth, the speed of its links to other chips, from 600 to 400 GB/s.

    NVIDIA Form 8-K, 31 August 2022www.sec.gov

  4. 7 Oct 2022in force 21 Oct 2022US (BIS)

    US export control · Rule

    October 2022 rules on advanced computing and semiconductor equipment

    China lost access to top chips, the tools to make them, and American engineers.

    BIS created ECCN 3A090 and imposed China-wide controls on advanced chips, capturing the A100 and H100. The controls covered chips with a total processing performance (TPP), the rules' measure of computing power, of 4,800 or more, combined with interconnect bandwidth of 600 GB/s or more. New foreign direct product rules extended the chip controls to such chips and computers made outside the United States with US technology or software. Equipment controls covered fabs making logic at 16/14 nm or below or with non-planar transistors, DRAM at 18 nm half-pitch or below and NAND with 128 layers or more. US persons needed a BIS license to support advanced chipmaking in China. The interim final rule was published on 13 October. Parts of §§742.6 and 744.23 and the new equipment ECCN 3B090 took effect on 7 October, and §744.6 on 12 October. The chip ECCNs 3A090 and 4A090, the direct product rules and the Entity List changes took effect on 21 October.

  5. 9 Nov 2022Germany (government)

    Other governments · Screening

    Germany blocks Chinese investment in two chipmakers

    Berlin vetoed a Chinese-owned firm's purchase of Elmos's chip factory and blocked investment in ERS Electronic.

    The German government blocked Chinese investment in two domestic semiconductor producers after the deals raised concerns about national security and the flow of sensitive know-how to China. It vetoed the takeover of the chip factory of Elmos, a company based in Dortmund, by Silex, a Swedish subsidiary of the Chinese group Sai Microelectronics. Economy Minister Robert Habeck said that in the semiconductor sector the government wanted to protect the technological and economic sovereignty of Germany and Europe. Sai Microelectronics said it deeply regretted the decision.

    www.reuters.com

    The British government ordered Nexperia, a Chinese-owned technology company headquartered in the Netherlands, to sell at least 86 percent of Newport Wafer Fab, Britain's biggest microchip factory.     Section 5949 of the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for fiscal 2023 covers semiconductors designed or made by SMIC, ChangXin Memory (CXMT) or Yangtze Memory (YMTC), or by their subsidiaries and successors.   7. 21 Sep 2023EU (Parliament and Council)

    Industrial policy · Policy

    European Chips Act enters into force

    The EU set a goal of 20 percent of the global chip market in 2030 and put €3.3 billion of EU funds into chip research and pilot lines.

    The European Chips Act entered into force on 21 September 2023, with the aim of doubling the EU's share of the global semiconductor market to 20 percent in 2030. Its first pillar, the Chips for Europe Initiative, has €3.3 billion of EU funds, which member states are expected to match. License Exception AIA allowed shipments to eighteen allies and the United States, the nineteen destinations listed in supplement no. 5 to part 740. License Exception LPP let each recipient almost everywhere else receive chips totaling up to 26.9 million TPP a year, about 1,700 H100-class GPUs. Under ECCN 4E091, it controlled for the first time the model weights of closed frontier AI models, the trained numbers that make up each model.     China paused its widest rare earth controls, including the 0.1 percent rule, until 10 November 2026.

    MOFCOM and the General Administration of Customs suspended six export control announcements issued in October 2025, from 7 November 2025 until 10 November 2026. They are MOFCOM and Customs Announcements 2025 Nos. 55, 56, 57 and 58 and MOFCOM Announcements 2025 Nos. 61 and 62. No. 61 is the rule that claimed jurisdiction over foreign goods with 0.1 percent or more Chinese rare earths by value.

    MOFCOM and GAC Announcement 2025 No. 70www.mofcom.gov.cn

  25. 9 Nov 2025China (MOFCOM)

    China · Rule

    China suspends its ban on gallium, germanium and antimony exports to the US

    China paused its December 2024 ban on mineral exports to the US until 27 November 2026.

    MOFCOM suspended paragraph 2 of Announcement 2024 No. 46 from 9 November 2025 until 27 November 2026. That paragraph said exports to the United States of dual-use items related to gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials would in principle not be licensed. It also set stricter end-user and end-use checks on graphite exports to the United States.

    MOFCOM Announcement 2025 No. 72www.mofcom.gov.cn

  26. 10 Nov 2025US (BIS)

    US export control · Rule

    US suspends the affiliates rule for one year under the truce

    Both sides suspended their broadest measures for a year, and China agreed to issue general licenses.

    After the Trump-Xi meeting in Busan on 30 October 2025, BIS suspended the affiliates rule from 10 November 2025 until 9 November 2026. The same rule brings the affiliates rule back on 10 November 2026 unless the suspension is extended. China had suspended its own October 2025 export controls on 7 November and its ban on mineral exports to the United States on 9 November. China also agreed to issue general licenses, which cover repeated exports without a separate approval for each, for US end users and their suppliers.

    90 FR 50857 · 15 CFR 744.11(a)(1)www.federalregister.gov

  27. 15 Nov 2025EU (European Commission)

    Other governments · Rule

    EU adds Dutch chip-tool controls to its own control list

    Dutch national controls became EU-wide, with no change for ASML's own shipments.

    The European Union added certain Dutch national controls to the EU Control List in November 2025, extending a license requirement for specific semiconductor manufacturing equipment to all member states. ASML said in its 2025 annual report that the requirement covers its DUV immersion lithography systems when they are exported outside the EU. It said the change made no difference to the company, because those products already required an export license from the Netherlands.

    Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2003www.sec.gov

  28. 8 Dec 2025US (White House)

    US export control · License policy

    Trump clears H200 sales to China

    China could buy the chip, but only after US testing and a 25 percent tariff.

    President Trump announced that the United States would allow the H200 and similar products to be shipped to approved customers in China. BIS announced the implementing rule on 13 January 2026, and it took effect on publication on 15 January. It moved license applications for the Nvidia H200, the AMD MI325X and similar chips from a presumption of denial, under which they are normally refused, to case-by-case review. The applicant must show that the exports will not reduce the global semiconductor capacity available to US customers. It must also show that the Chinese purchaser has adopted export compliance procedures, including customer screening, and that the item has passed independent third-party testing in the United States. Nvidia's filings state that the licenses require each H200 to pass a US inspection before shipment. The filings say that, as a result, any H200 shipped under the program is subject to a 25 percent tariff on importation into the United States. Nvidia says it has been unable to pass the tariff on to customers.

    BIS press release, 13 January 2026www.bis.gov

202610 moves

  1. 14 Jan 2026in force 15 Jan 2026US (White House)

    Industrial policy · Policy

    Section 232 proclamation puts a 25 percent tariff on advanced AI chips

    A 25 percent tariff applies to advanced chips that pass through the United States for use elsewhere.

    A presidential proclamation under Section 232, which lets the president restrict imports that threaten national security, imposed a 25 percent tariff from 12:01 a.m. on 15 January 2026. It covers a narrow set of advanced computing semiconductors, and products containing them, that pass through the United States but are not destined for US use. The covered chips fall in two bands. The first is chips of 14,000 to 17,500 total processing performance (TPP), a measure of computing power, with 4,500 to 5,000 GB/s of DRAM bandwidth. The second is chips of 20,800 to 21,100 TPP with 5,800 to 6,200 GB/s. These bands capture the Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X. Nvidia's H200 licenses require each China-bound chip to pass an inspection in the United States before shipment, so every licensed H200 is imported first and pays the tariff. Eight use-based exemptions cover US data centers, R&D, start-ups, repairs, consumer and industrial uses and the public sector. The proclamation ordered a review of data-center chips by 1 July 2026 and signaled a second phase with higher rates and tariff relief for companies that invest in US chip production.

    91 FR 2443 (Proclamation 11002)www.whitehouse.gov

  2. 15 Jan 2026US (BIS)

    US export control · License policy

    H200-class chips move to case-by-case licensing for China

    BIS began case-by-case licensing to China for a band of chips below the top tier, but not for Nvidia's newer Blackwell chips.

    BIS announced the policy on 13 January 2026 and the rule took effect on publication, 15 January. It shifted license review from a presumption of denial to case-by-case review for exports of certain advanced computing chips from the United States to China and Macau. The covered chips have total processing performance below 21,000 and total DRAM bandwidth below 6,500 GB/s, the band covering the Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X. Approval requires certifications of adequate US supply, independent third-party testing inside US customs territory, and know-your-customer and remote-access safeguards. Because the testing condition routes the chips through the United States, they also incur the 25 percent Section 232 tariff. Nvidia's newer Blackwell-class chips remain outside the policy. The rule changed only the China and Macau branch of the license policy, at 742.6(b)(10)(iii)(A)(1). It left the worldwide license requirement and the presumption of approval for the destinations in supplement no. 5 as they stood.

    91 FR 1684 · 15 CFR 742.6(b)(10)(iii)www.federalregister.gov

  3. 15 Jan 2026US and Taiwan (AIT and TECRO)

    Industrial policy · Policy

    US-Taiwan memorandum of understanding on investment

    Taiwan won tariff relief on car parts, timber and aircraft components and pledged $250 billion of US investment.

    The American Institute in Taiwan and the Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office, which serve as the two sides' unofficial embassies, signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) on Taiwan-US investment. In it, the United States committed to modify certain Section 232 tariffs on Taiwanese goods. Commerce and the US Trade Representative implemented the tariff elements on 28 May 2026. They amended the tariff schedule for Taiwanese automobile parts, timber, lumber and wood derivative products, and removed derivative Section 232 steel, aluminum and copper tariffs from Taiwanese aircraft components. The two offices signed a broader Agreement on Reciprocal Trade on 12 February 2026, but it had not entered into force when the implementing notice was published. The notice records two commitments under the MOU. Taiwan will provide credit guarantees for up to $250 billion of corporate credit. Taiwanese semiconductor and technology firms will make $250 billion of new direct investment in the United States.

    www.federalregister.gov

  4. 12 Feb 2026US (BIS)

    US export control · Enforcement

    Applied Materials pays about $252 million for shipments to SMIC

    Applied Materials paid twice what the shipments were worth, the second largest penalty in BIS history.

    BIS announced a settlement of about $252 million with Applied Materials and its Korean subsidiary. The case concerned unlicensed reexports of ion implanters, chipmaking tools classified under ECCN 3B991, to SMIC after SMIC was added to the Entity List. The equipment was built in Massachusetts and routed through Korea. The shipments were worth about $126 million, so the penalty is twice the transaction value. That is the most the law allows, and the penalty is the second largest in BIS history. Applied Materials agreed to multiple compliance audits and annual certifications, and the employees responsible no longer work for the company.

    15 CFR part 764www.bis.gov

  5. 19 Mar 2026US (DOJ)

    US export control · Enforcement

    Super Micro co-founder charged over AI servers diverted to China

    Prosecutors allege that at least $510 million of AI servers reached China through false papers and layered transshipment.

    Federal prosecutors in the Southern District of New York charged Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw, Taiwan-based general manager Ruei-Tsang Chang and broker Ting-Wei Sun. They are charged with conspiring to violate the Export Control Reform Act, to smuggle goods and to defraud the United States. Prosecutors allege that a buyer purchased about $2.5 billion of servers from the manufacturer in 2024 and 2025 on false end-user records. They allege that at least $510 million of those servers were diverted to China between late April and mid-May 2025. The scheme allegedly relied on layered transshipment and on staged dummy servers to deceive auditors. Liaw resigned from the Super Micro board the next day and pleaded not guilty on 1 April 2026.

    www.justice.gov

  6. 10 Jul 2026US (BIS)

    US export control · Rule

    UAE moved to Country Group A:5

    UAE government agencies, approved companies on a US list and eight named US AI firms can now receive advanced chips without a license.

    BIS removed the United Arab Emirates from Country Groups D:3 and D:4, the US lists of countries of concern for chemical and biological weapons and for missiles. It added the UAE to A:5, a group of close US partners that face fewer export controls. The move made the UAE eligible for Strategic Trade Authorization and for license exceptions TMP, GOV, TSU, AVS and APR for chemical, biological and missile-technology controlled items. Advanced AI chips and the computers that contain them, under ECCNs 3A090.a and 4A090.a, still need a license. They need none when shipped to UAE government agencies, to approved commercial entities listed in a new Supplement No. 8, or to US-headquartered AI companies and their UAE subsidiaries. The rule names eight such companies: Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI. The rule wrote into regulation the country-by-country approach that replaced the AI Diffusion Rule's country caps.

    91 FR 43034 · 15 CFR 742.6(a)(6); 740www.federalregister.gov

  7. 15 Jul 2026India (Union Cabinet)

    Industrial policy · Policy

    India approves Semicon 2.0

    India budgeted ₹1,27,500 crore for a second chip program after approving twelve plants under the first.

    India's Union Cabinet approved Semicon 2.0, a program for the country's chip design and manufacturing industry with a budget of ₹1,27,500 crore. Its six pillars are chip design, machines and materials, new fabs, assembly and packaging units, research and development, and talent. The government said India's first fab is scheduled to be commissioned in 2028. Under Semicon 1.0, twelve manufacturing units had been approved with a cumulative investment of over ₹1.64 lakh crore. They include one silicon fab, one silicon carbide fab, a gallium nitride micro LED display fab and nine packaging units. Micron, Kaynes and CG Semi have started commercial production.

    www.pib.gov.in

  8. 6 Aug 2026in force 4 Dec 2026US (White House)

    Industrial policy · Policy

    Proclamation 11052 sets a price floor and an extra duty on polysilicon imports

    Imported silicon wafers face a price floor and an extra duty from December 2026, with relief for firms building US plants.

    A presidential proclamation signed on 6 August 2026 set a minimum import price of $100 per kilogram for polysilicon ingots and wafers. Polysilicon is the purified silicon that chip and solar wafers are made from. The proclamation also set an extra 15 percent duty on imported ingots and other listed products made from polysilicon. Both measures start on 4 December 2026. Firms with Commerce-approved plans to build US polysilicon, ingot, wafer or solar cell plants, with construction starting by 20 January 2029, can import equipment and some of those products without the new duties. A Commerce rule published on 24 September 2026, meant to stop stockpiling before the duties start, lists doped single-crystal silicon wafers among the products it covers.

    91 FR 51975 (Proclamation 11052)www.federalregister.gov

  9. 26 Aug 2026China (PRC government) and Nvidia

    China · Countermeasure

    PRC restrictions leave the H200 licenses largely unused

    Beijing restricted the sales, so Nvidia shipped a fraction of the licensed H200s and took a charge on unsold inventory.

    Nvidia's quarterly filing for the period to 26 July 2026 records that the US government began granting licenses in February 2026 to ship small amounts of H200 to specific China-based customers. But, in the company's words, "such sales were restricted by the PRC government, and we have been unable to sell all the products for which we have licenses". Nvidia took a $0.4 billion charge in the first half of its fiscal 2027, the six months to 26 July 2026, for excess H200 inventory and purchase obligations. It shipped only a fraction of what the licenses allowed, and those shipments came to less than 1 percent of data-center revenue in the quarter. Customers headquartered in China, including Hong Kong, accounted for $7.9 billion of the quarter's $96.2 billion of revenue, against $4.0 billion a year earlier. Beijing has not published the measures behind its restrictions.

    NVIDIA Form 10-Q, Q2 FY2027www.sec.gov

  10. 7 Sep 2026China (MOFCOM)

    China · Trade remedy

    China hits Japanese dichlorosilane with duties of up to 99.2 percent

    Chinese importers must post deposits of up to 99.2 percent on a Japanese gas that chip fabs use to lay down thin films.

    China's commerce ministry, MOFCOM, issued a preliminary anti-dumping ruling against Japanese dichlorosilane, a specialty gas used for thin-film deposition in chipmaking. From 8 September 2026, importers must post deposits with Chinese customs at rates of 80.8 to 99.2 percent, pending a final ruling. The 99.2 percent rate applies to Shin-Etsu Chemical and all non-cooperating exporters. The investigation opened on 7 January 2026 after a complaint from the Chinese producer Tangshan Sanfu Electronic Materials. MOFCOM said the complaint's preliminary evidence showed import prices falling a cumulative 31 percent from 2022 to 2024. Japan protested the measure. The investigation is normally due to end by 7 January 2027 and can be extended by six months.

    MOFCOM Announcement 2026 No. 37www.mofcom.gov.cn
